questions.q: What is the normal mean diameter and central thickness of a mature human biconcave erythrocyte?
options: Diameter 7.2 to 7.8 micrometers and central thickness about 1 micrometer
Diameter 12 to 15 micrometers and central thickness 4 micrometers
Diameter 2 to 3 micrometers and central thickness 0.2 micrometers
Diameter 18 to 20 micrometers and central thickness 6 micrometers
questions.explain: Mature human red blood cells are biconcave discs measuring roughly 7.2 to 7.8 micrometers in diameter, 2.5 micrometers thick at the rim, and 1 micrometer thick at the center.

open.q: State the normal diameter and central thickness of a mature human red blood cell in micrometers.
accept: 7.5 micrometers diameter and 1 micrometer central thickness
7.2-7.8 um diameter and 1 um central thickness

questions.q: Which physiological advantage is conferred by the biconcave disc shape of mature red blood cells?
options: It increases DNA transcription rate inside the erythrocyte
It maximizes surface area-to-volume ratio for rapid gas diffusion and allows deformability through narrow capillaries
It enables active amoeboid diapedesis across venular walls
It provides storage space for glycogen granules and mitochondria
questions.explain: The biconcave geometry provides about 30% extra surface area relative to a sphere of equal volume, accelerating O2 and CO2 diffusion and letting the 7.5 micrometer cell fold through 3 micrometer splenic and capillary channels.

open.q: State two functional advantages of the biconcave disc shape of mature erythrocytes.
accept: High surface area-to-volume ratio for gas diffusion and flexibility to squeeze through narrow capillaries
Faster gas exchange and high deformability

questions.q: Which cytoskeletal protein forms the hexagonal submembranous meshwork responsible for maintaining erythrocyte biconcave shape and membrane deformability?
options: Myosin heavy chain
Tubulin
Spectrin
Vimentin
questions.explain: Spectrin tetramers linked to actin and anchored to integral membrane proteins (band 3 and glycophorin) via ankyrin and band 4.1 maintain erythrocyte elasticity; defects cause hereditary spherocytosis or elliptocytosis.

open.q: Name the principal cytoskeletal protein lining the inner surface of the red blood cell membrane that maintains its biconcave shape and elasticity.

questions.q: Because mature mammalian erythrocytes lack mitochondria, through which metabolic pathway do they generate ATP?
options: Citric acid (Krebs) cycle
Beta-oxidation of long-chain fatty acids
Electron transport chain oxidative phosphorylation
Anaerobic glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof pathway)
questions.explain: Mature RBCs have no nuclei, ribosomes, or mitochondria, so they rely exclusively on anaerobic glycolysis (Embden-Meyerhof pathway) for ATP and the hexose monophosphate shunt for NADPH.

open.q: By which metabolic pathway do mature red blood cells generate ATP in the absence of mitochondria?

questions.q: What is the normal red blood cell count in healthy adult males and adult females?
options: Males: 4.5 to 6.0 million/mm3; Females: 4.0 to 5.5 million/mm3
Males: 1.5 to 2.5 million/mm3; Females: 1.0 to 2.0 million/mm3
Males: 8.0 to 10.0 million/mm3; Females: 7.5 to 9.5 million/mm3
Males: 4,000 to 11,000/mm3; Females: 3,500 to 10,000/mm3
questions.explain: Normal adult RBC count averages ~5.2 million/mm3 (4.5-6.0 x 10^6/uL) in males and ~4.7 million/mm3 (4.0-5.5 x 10^6/uL) in females, largely because testosterone stimulates erythropoiesis while estrogens slightly inhibit it.

open.q: Give the normal reference ranges for red blood cell count in healthy adult males and females.

questions.q: In which anatomical site does erythropoiesis primarily occur during the third trimester of fetal life and throughout adult life?
options: Yolk sac mesoderm
Red bone marrow
Splenic white pulp
Thymic cortex
questions.explain: Erythropoiesis shifts from the yolk sac (mesoblastic phase, weeks 3-8) to the fetal liver and spleen (hepatic phase, months 2-5), and finally to red bone marrow (myeloid phase) from the last trimester onward.

open.q: What is the primary site of erythropoiesis in healthy adults?

questions.q: During normal erythropoiesis in the bone marrow, at which developmental stage is the nucleus extruded from the developing erythroid cell?
options: Proerythroblast
Basophilic normoblast
Orthochromatic normoblast (late normoblast)
Reticulocyte
questions.explain: As hemoglobin accumulates, the nucleus shrinks and becomes pyknotic in the orthochromatic (acidophilic) normoblast before being extruded to form an anucleate reticulocyte.

open.q: At which stage of erythroid maturation is the pyknotic nucleus extruded from the cell?

questions.q: What is the normal reticulocyte count in peripheral venous blood, and what does an elevated reticulocyte count indicate in an anemic patient?
options: 10% to 15%; indicates bone marrow aplasia
0.01% to 0.05%; indicates iron deficiency
20% to 30%; indicates vitamin B12 deficiency
0.5% to 2.0%; indicates an active, appropriate bone marrow erythropoietic response
questions.explain: Reticulocytes normally constitute 0.5% to 2.0% of circulating red cells and mature into erythrocytes within 1 to 2 days; a high reticulocyte count in anemia signals brisk marrow regeneration (e.g., after hemolysis or acute hemorrhage).

open.q: State the normal peripheral blood reticulocyte percentage and what a high count signifies in a patient with anemia.
accept: 0.5% to 2.0%; indicates increased bone marrow RBC production

questions.q: Which organs produce erythropoietin (EPO) in adults and in the fetus, respectively?
options: Peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in adults (~85-90%) and hepatocytes in the fetus
Juxtaglomerular granular cells in adults and alveolar macrophages in the fetus
Adrenal cortex in adults and bone marrow stromal cells in the fetus
Splenic red pulp in adults and pancreatic acinar cells in the fetus
questions.explain: In adults, 85% to 90% of erythropoietin is synthesized by renal peritubular capillary endothelial/interstitial cells in response to hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1/2), while 10% to 15% (and the bulk in fetal life) comes from the liver.

open.q: Name the primary site of erythropoietin production in adults and its major site during fetal life.
accept: Kidney (renal peritubular interstitial cells) in adults and liver in the fetus
Kidneys in adults, liver in fetus

questions.q: What is the primary physiological stimulus that increases erythropoietin (EPO) gene transcription and secretion?
options: Hypercapnia (elevated arterial PCO2)
Tissue hypoxia (reduced renal oxygen delivery)
Hyperglycemia
Elevated serum ferritin
questions.explain: Hypoxia stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-2alpha), which binds the hypoxia response element on the EPO gene in renal peritubular cells, boosting EPO secretion to stimulate CFU-E proliferation.

open.q: What is the main physiological stimulus for increased erythropoietin secretion?
accept: Reduced oxygen delivery to the kidneys

questions.sub: Maturation Factors: Vitamin B12, Folate, and Iron
questions.q: Why does deficiency of either vitamin B12 or folic acid produce megaloblastic anemia?
options: Both are structural subunits of the porphyrin ring in heme
Both are required to synthesize spectrin in the red cell cytoskeleton
Both are essential cofactors for thymidylate and DNA synthesis, slowing nuclear division while cytoplasmic hemoglobin synthesis continues
Both directly activate renal erythropoietin receptors
questions.explain: Vitamin B12 and folate are required for one-carbon transfer reactions needed to synthesize thymidine triphosphate (dTTP) for DNA replication; impaired DNA synthesis delays nuclear division, yielding large macrocytic precursors (megaloblasts).

open.q: Explain why deficiency of vitamin B12 or folic acid leads to megaloblastic anemia.
accept: Impaired DNA synthesis delays nuclear maturation while cytoplasmic RNA and hemoglobin synthesis proceed normally
Defective DNA and thymidylate synthesis causes nuclear-cytoplasmic asynchrony

questions.sub: Maturation Factors: Vitamin B12, Folate, and Iron
questions.q: Where is vitamin B12 (cobalamin) bound to intrinsic factor absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract?
options: Gastric fundus
Duodenal bulb
Proximal jejunum
Terminal ileum
questions.explain: Gastric parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which binds vitamin B12 in the duodenum and facilitates receptor-mediated uptake via cubilin receptors specifically in the terminal ileum.

open.q: In which specific segment of the small intestine is the vitamin B12-intrinsic factor complex absorbed?

questions.sub: Maturation Factors: Vitamin B12, Folate, and Iron
questions.q: Why must clinicians distinguish vitamin B12 deficiency from folate deficiency before treating a patient with megaloblastic anemia using folic acid alone?
options: Folic acid corrects the hematologic anemia of B12 deficiency but fails to prevent or reverse subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord
Folic acid precipitates acute hemolytic crisis in vitamin B12 deficiency
Folic acid blocks iron absorption in the duodenum
Folic acid suppresses endogenous erythropoietin secretion
questions.explain: High-dose folate bypasses the methylfolate trap to restore DNA synthesis and resolve megaloblastic anemia, but vitamin B12 is uniquely required for myelin maintenance via methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, so neurological damage progresses if B12 is not replaced.

open.q: What clinical danger arises if a patient with vitamin B12 deficiency is treated solely with folic acid?
accept: Anemia improves while irreversible neurological degeneration progresses
Masks the anemia without preventing subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord

questions.sub: Maturation Factors: Vitamin B12, Folate, and Iron
questions.q: In which oxidation state is dietary iron absorbed across the duodenal brush border via divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1), and which protein transports iron in plasma?
options: Ferric (Fe3+) state; transported by ferritin
Ferrous (Fe2+) state; transported by transferrin
Ferrous (Fe2+) state; transported by ceruloplasmin
Ferric (Fe3+) state; transported by haptoglobin
questions.explain: Gastric acid and duodenal cytochrome b reduce dietary Fe3+ to soluble Fe2+ for uptake via DMT1; after export through ferroportin and oxidation by hephaestin, Fe3+ binds transferrin for plasma transport.

open.q: In what ionic valence state is iron absorbed by duodenal enterocytes, and what plasma protein transports iron in the blood?

questions.sub: Maturation Factors: Vitamin B12, Folate, and Iron
questions.q: How does the hepatic peptide hormone hepcidin regulate systemic iron homeostasis?
options: It stimulates duodenal ferroportin expression to maximize iron absorption
It converts ferric iron to ferrous iron in the stomach
It binds and induces degradation of ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages, reducing plasma iron levels
It increases transferrin receptor synthesis on erythroblasts
questions.explain: Hepcidin is the master negative regulator of iron release: it internalizes and degrades ferroportin on duodenal enterocytes and splenic macrophages, blocking dietary iron absorption and iron recycling during iron overload or inflammation.

open.q: Explain the mechanism by which hepcidin lowers serum iron concentration.
accept: Binds and degrades ferroportin on enterocytes and macrophages
Inhibits ferroportin-mediated iron export from gut cells and macrophages

questions.q: What is the globin chain composition of normal adult hemoglobin A (HbA), hemoglobin A2 (HbA2), and fetal hemoglobin (HbF)?
options: HbA: alpha2-gamma2; HbA2: alpha2-beta2; HbF: alpha2-delta2
HbA: beta2-gamma2; HbA2: alpha2-beta2; HbF: alpha2-epsilon2
HbA: alpha2-delta2; HbA2: alpha2-gamma2; HbF: alpha2-beta2
HbA: alpha2-beta2; HbA2: alpha2-delta2; HbF: alpha2-gamma2
questions.explain: Normal adult hemoglobin consists of ~96-98% HbA (alpha2-beta2) and ~2-3% HbA2 (alpha2-delta2), whereas fetal hemoglobin HbF (alpha2-gamma2) predominates in utero and drops below 1% after infancy.

open.q: State the globin polypeptide chain compositions of HbA, HbA2, and HbF.
accept: HbA: alpha2 beta2, HbA2: alpha2 delta2, HbF: alpha2 gamma2

questions.q: How many oxygen molecules can one fully saturated hemoglobin tetramer bind, and to which chemical component does oxygen attach?
options: 4 molecules of O2, bound reversibly to the ferrous (Fe2+) iron atom at the center of each of the 4 heme rings
2 molecules of O2, bound covalently to the beta-globin chains
4 molecules of O2, bound to ferric (Fe3+) iron in the porphyrin ring
8 molecules of O2, bound to histidine residues on alpha-globin
questions.explain: Each hemoglobin molecule has four polypeptide subunits, each housing a heme group with a central ferrous (Fe2+) ion capable of reversibly binding one O2 molecule (oxygenation, not oxidation), totaling 4 O2 molecules (1.34 mL O2 per gram of Hb).

open.q: How many oxygen molecules does one fully saturated hemoglobin molecule carry, and to which specific atom and oxidation state do they bind?
accept: 4 O2 molecules bound to ferrous (Fe2+) iron in heme
Four oxygen molecules attached to Fe2+ in the four heme groups

questions.q: Why does fetal hemoglobin (HbF) have a higher affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin (HbA)?
options: HbF contains six heme groups instead of four
The gamma-globin chains of HbF bind 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG) much less avidly than beta-globin chains
HbF maintains iron in the ferric (Fe3+) state
HbF lacks histidine residues near the heme pocket
questions.explain: Gamma chains replace a positively charged histidine (His143) in beta chains with neutral serine, reducing electrostatic binding to negatively charged 2,3-BPG; this shifts the HbF dissociation curve left, aiding placental oxygen transfer from mother to fetus.

open.q: Explain the molecular reason why fetal hemoglobin (HbF) has a higher oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin (HbA).
accept: HbF has lower affinity for 2,3-BPG than HbA
Gamma chains bind 2,3-BPG less strongly than beta chains

questions.q: What occurs when the ferrous iron (Fe2+) of hemoglobin is oxidized to the ferric state (Fe3+) by nitrites, dapsone, or oxidant drugs?
options: Carboxyhemoglobin forms with increased oxygen unloading to tissues
Carbaminohemoglobin forms and causes respiratory alkalosis
Methemoglobin forms, which cannot bind oxygen and shifts the dissociation curve of remaining heme sites to the left
Sulfhemoglobin forms and increases hematocrit acutely
questions.explain: Oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ produces methemoglobin, which cannot bind O2 and increases the O2 affinity of remaining Fe2+ subunits (left shift), causing chocolate-brown blood and functional tissue hypoxia; NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase normally reduces it back to Fe2+.

open.q: What abnormal hemoglobin derivative is formed when heme Fe2+ is oxidized to Fe3+, and how does this affect oxygen transport?
accept: Methemoglobin; it cannot bind O2 and impairs O2 unloading from remaining subunits

questions.q: Carbon monoxide (CO) binds to hemoglobin with an affinity approximately 200 to 250 times greater than that of oxygen. Besides occupying oxygen-binding sites, how else does carboxyhemoglobin impair tissue oxygenation?
options: It shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve sharply to the right
It accelerates renal erythropoietin degradation within minutes
It oxidizes all four heme groups to methemoglobin
It shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left, preventing unloading of bound oxygen in peripheral tissues
questions.explain: CO locks hemoglobin in the high-affinity R (relaxed) conformation, shifting the O2 dissociation curve leftward and making it hyperbolic so tissues cannot extract whatever O2 remains bound.

open.q: State two mechanisms by which carbon monoxide (CO) causes severe tissue hypoxia.
accept: Competes with O2 at heme binding sites with ~240x affinity and shifts the O2 dissociation curve left to impair unloading
Blocks O2 binding and prevents O2 release in tissues via a leftward shift

questions.q: What is the normal lifespan of a circulating human erythrocyte, and where are senescent red blood cells primarily destroyed?
options: 120 days; destroyed by macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system, chiefly in the spleen
30 days; destroyed by renal tubular epithelial cells
7 to 10 days; destroyed by pulmonary capillary endothelium
365 days; destroyed by circulating neutrophils
questions.explain: Without a nucleus to synthesize new enzymes, erythrocyte glycolytic and antioxidant enzymes decline over ~120 days; rigid, aged RBCs become trapped in splenic red pulp cords of Billroth and are phagocytosed by macrophages.

open.q: State the average lifespan of a mature human erythrocyte and the primary organ where senescent red cells are removed.

questions.q: During macrophage degradation of heme from senescent red blood cells, which enzyme converts heme into biliverdin, carbon monoxide, and free iron?
options: Biliverdin reductase
Heme oxygenase
UDP-glucuronosyltransferase
Ferrochelatase
questions.explain: Microsomal heme oxygenase cleaves the porphyrin ring to yield green biliverdin, endogenous carbon monoxide (CO), and Fe2+ (recycled via transferrin); biliverdin reductase then reduces biliverdin to unconjugated bilirubin.

open.q: Name the enzyme in macrophages that cleaves heme into biliverdin, carbon monoxide, and iron.

questions.q: How is water-insoluble unconjugated bilirubin transported in plasma to the liver, and which hepatic enzyme conjugates it for biliary excretion?
options: Bound to haptoglobin; conjugated by glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Bound to transferrin; conjugated by biliverdin reductase
Bound to serum albumin; conjugated with glucuronic acid by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1)
Dissolved freely in plasma water; conjugated by carbonic anhydrase
questions.explain: Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin binds albumin in blood, enters hepatocytes, and is conjugated with glucuronic acid via UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1) into water-soluble conjugated (direct) bilirubin diglucuronide excreted in bile.

open.q: Name the plasma carrier protein for unconjugated bilirubin and the hepatic enzyme that conjugates it with glucuronic acid.

questions.q: Which formula correctly defines Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) and what is its normal adult reference range?
options: MCV = (Hemoglobin / RBC count) x 10; normal 27 to 32 pg
MCV = (Hemoglobin / Hematocrit) x 100; normal 32 to 36 g/dL
MCV = (RBC count / Hematocrit) x 100; normal 40 to 50 fL
MCV = (Hematocrit % / RBC count in millions/uL) x 10; normal 80 to 100 fL
questions.explain: MCV measures average red cell size in femtoliters (fL): MCV = (Hct % x 10) / RBC count (millions/uL), normally 80-100 fL (less than 80 fL = microcytic; greater than 100 fL = macrocytic).

open.q: Give the formula and normal adult reference range for Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV).
accept: (Hematocrit % x 10) / RBC count in millions/uL; 80 to 100 fL

questions.q: A patient has a hemoglobin concentration of 9.0 g/dL, hematocrit of 30%, and RBC count of 4.5 million/uL. What are the calculated MCV and MCHC?
options: MCV = 66.7 fL (microcytic) and MCHC = 30.0 g/dL (hypochromic)
MCV = 90.0 fL (normocytic) and MCHC = 34.0 g/dL (normochromic)
MCV = 110.0 fL (macrocytic) and MCHC = 35.0 g/dL (normochromic)
MCV = 66.7 fL (microcytic) and MCHC = 36.0 g/dL (hyperchromic)
questions.explain: MCV = (30 x 10) / 4.5 = 66.7 fL (microcytic, normal 80-100 fL); MCHC = (Hb / Hct %) x 100 = (9.0 / 30) x 100 = 30.0 g/dL (hypochromic, normal 32-36 g/dL), typical of iron deficiency anemia.

open.q: Calculate MCV and MCHC for a patient with Hb 9.0 g/dL, Hct 30%, and RBC count 4.5 million/uL.

questions.sub: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) and Osmotic Fragility
questions.q: What is the primary physical mechanism that accelerates the Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) during acute inflammation or pregnancy?
options: Increased red blood cell diameter due to megaloblastic change
Elevated plasma fibrinogen and immunoglobulins neutralize negative RBC surface zeta potential, promoting rouleaux formation
Decreased plasma viscosity due to hypoalbuminemia
Increased osmotic fragility causing rapid intravascular hemolysis
questions.explain: Sialic acid in the RBC glycocalyx creates a repulsive negative zeta potential; positively charged acute-phase proteins like fibrinogen neutralize this charge so RBCs stack like coins (rouleaux) and fall faster.

open.q: Why does elevated plasma fibrinogen increase the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)?
accept: Neutralizes negative RBC surface charge (zeta potential) and promotes rouleaux formation
Causes red blood cells to stack into rouleaux which sediment faster

questions.sub: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) and Osmotic Fragility
questions.q: In which hematologic condition is the Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) characteristically markedly reduced (near 0 mm/hr) even in the presence of inflammation?
options: Multiple myeloma
Rheumatoid arthritis
Sickle cell anemia and polycythemia vera
Iron deficiency anemia
questions.explain: Poikilocytes such as sickled cells cannot stack efficiently into linear rouleaux, while extreme polycythemia increases blood viscosity and crowds cells, keeping ESR very low.

open.q: Name two hematologic conditions in which the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is characteristically very low.
accept: Polycythemia vera and sickle cell disease

questions.sub: Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) and Osmotic Fragility
questions.q: In an osmotic fragility test, red blood cells from a patient with hereditary spherocytosis begin to hemolyze at 0.65% NaCl (compared to normal onset at ~0.45% NaCl). Why do spherocytes show increased osmotic fragility?
options: They contain excess intracellular hemoglobin crystals
Their cell membranes are completely permeable to sodium ions
They have an abnormally high surface area-to-volume ratio
They have a reduced surface area-to-volume ratio and cannot expand further when water enters in hypotonic saline
questions.explain: Loss of membrane spectrin/ankyrin causes RBCs to shed membrane fragments and become spherical; spheres already hold maximum volume for their surface area, so even mild hypotonic swelling ruptures them.

open.q: Why is osmotic fragility increased in hereditary spherocytosis?
accept: Reduced surface area-to-volume ratio limits swelling capacity in hypotonic solutions
Spherocytes lack excess membrane surface area to accommodate osmotic water influx

questions.q: A 19-year-old Nigerian undergraduate presents with severe bone pain crisis, dactylitis history, jaundice, and sickled erythrocytes on peripheral blood smear after a bout of malaria and dehydration. Which exact amino acid substitution in the beta-globin chain causes sickle cell disease (HbS)?
options: Replacement of hydrophilic glutamate with hydrophobic valine at position 6 of the beta-globin chain
Replacement of valine with glutamate at position 6 of the alpha-globin chain
Replacement of glutamate with lysine at position 6 of the beta-globin chain
Deletion of all four alpha-globin genes on chromosome 16
questions.explain: A single point mutation (GAG to GTG) substitutes nonpolar valine for polar glutamic acid at codon 6 of beta-globin; upon deoxygenation, hydrophobic valine residues polymerize into rigid fibers that distort RBCs into sickles.

open.q: State the exact molecular mutation in the beta-globin chain responsible for sickle cell hemoglobin (HbS).
accept: Substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta-globin chain

questions.q: A 22-year-old male medical student develops dark cola-colored urine, jaundice, and a sharp drop in hemoglobin 48 hours after taking primaquine for malaria prophylaxis. Peripheral smear shows bite cells and Heinz bodies. Which red cell enzyme deficiency explains this acute hemolytic crisis?
options: Pyruvate kinase deficiency
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency
Hexokinase deficiency
Ferrochelatase deficiency
questions.explain: G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway, generating NADPH needed to keep glutathione reduced (GSH); without GSH, oxidant drugs (primaquine, dapsone, sulfonamides) oxidize hemoglobin into precipitated Heinz bodies that splenic macrophages pluck out as bite cells.

open.q: Which X-linked erythrocyte enzyme deficiency predisposes to oxidative hemolysis with Heinz bodies and bite cells after exposure to primaquine or fava beans?

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman with chronic fatigue, glossitis, and numbness/tingling in her feet has macrocytic anemia (MCV 118 fL), hypersegmented neutrophils, and anti-parietal cell antibodies. Why does autoimmune gastritis lead to vitamin B12 deficiency?
options: Loss of chief cells stops pepsinogen activation
Loss of enteroendocrine G cells prevents gastrin release
Destruction of gastric parietal cells eliminates intrinsic factor secretion required for ileal B12 absorption
Hyperchlorhydria destroys dietary cobalamin in the stomach
questions.explain: Pernicious anemia is caused by autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells (or antibodies against intrinsic factor itself), preventing intrinsic factor-mediated absorption of vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum.

open.q: Explain the pathophysiological link between autoimmune destruction of gastric parietal cells in pernicious anemia and vitamin B12 deficiency.
accept: Loss of parietal cells stops intrinsic factor secretion needed for terminal ileal B12 absorption
Lack of intrinsic factor prevents vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum

questions.q: A 32-year-old farmer in Benue State presents with easy fatigability, koilonychia (spoon nails), pallor, and microcytic hypochromic anemia (MCV 68 fL, low serum ferritin, elevated TIBC). Which parasitic infection is a classic cause of this presentation via chronic occult gastrointestinal blood loss?
options: Plasmodium falciparum
Wuchereria bancrofti
Entamoeba histolytica
Hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus)
questions.explain: Hookworms attach to small intestinal mucosa and secrete anticoagulants while ingesting blood, causing chronic iron loss that depletes iron stores (low ferritin, high TIBC) and produces microcytic hypochromic anemia.

open.q: Name the intestinal helminth infection that commonly causes iron deficiency anemia via chronic mucosal blood loss in tropical regions.

questions.q: A 52-year-old man with end-stage chronic kidney disease has a normocytic normochromic anemia (Hb 7.8 g/dL, MCV 88 fL, low reticulocyte count). What is the primary mechanism of his anemia?
options: Deficient renal synthesis of erythropoietin (EPO)
Autoimmune destruction of circulating erythrocytes
Excessive hepatic hepcidin suppression
Intrinsic defect in bone marrow stem cell DNA synthesis
questions.explain: Progressive loss of renal peritubular interstitial cells markedly reduces erythropoietin secretion, leading to underproduction of red blood cells (hypoproliferative normocytic normochromic anemia) treated with recombinant human EPO.

open.q: What is the primary cause of normocytic normochromic anemia in patients with chronic kidney disease?

questions.q: How does primary polycythemia (polycythemia vera) differ hormonally from secondary physiological polycythemia seen at high altitude?
options: Both conditions exhibit markedly elevated serum erythropoietin levels
Polycythemia vera has low serum erythropoietin due to autonomous clonal marrow proliferation, whereas high-altitude polycythemia has elevated erythropoietin
Polycythemia vera is driven by hypoxia, whereas high-altitude polycythemia is caused by a JAK2 mutation
Both conditions show normal hematocrit with expanded plasma volume
questions.explain: Polycythemia vera is a myeloproliferative neoplasm (commonly JAK2 V617F positive) with autonomous RBC production that suppresses endogenous EPO via negative feedback, whereas chronic hypoxia raises EPO in secondary polycythemia.

open.q: Compare serum erythropoietin (EPO) levels in polycythemia vera versus secondary polycythemia caused by chronic hypoxia.
accept: Low EPO in polycythemia vera and high EPO in secondary polycythemia
Suppressed EPO in primary polycythemia, elevated EPO in secondary

questions.q: When hematocrit rises above 60% in severe polycythemia, why can tissue oxygen delivery actually become impaired despite the higher hemoglobin concentration?
options: Excess red blood cells cannot bind oxygen in pulmonary capillaries
High hematocrit eliminates plasma bicarbonate buffering
Exponentially rising blood viscosity increases vascular resistance and reduces blood flow
Polycythemic red cells lack 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate
questions.explain: Blood viscosity increases steeply once hematocrit exceeds ~55-60%, elevating total peripheral resistance and slowing capillary blood flow (Poiseuille's law) to a greater extent than arterial O2 content rises.

open.q: Why does severe polycythemia paradoxically impair blood flow and oxygen delivery to tissues?
accept: Markedly increased blood viscosity increases vascular resistance and decreases blood flow

questions.q: During acute intravascular hemolysis (such as an ABO-incompatible blood transfusion), which plasma protein binds free hemoglobin dimers to prevent renal tubular damage and urinary iron loss?
options: Ceruloplasmin
Transferrin
Transcortin
Haptoglobin
questions.explain: Haptoglobin binds free extracorpuscular hemoglobin in plasma, forming a large complex too big for glomerular filtration that is cleared by hepatic macrophages; thus, markedly decreased serum haptoglobin is a sensitive marker of intravascular hemolysis.

open.q: Name the plasma alpha-2 globulin that scavenges free hemoglobin released during intravascular hemolysis.
